data.title: Three things can come out
data.body: When a nucleus changes, it can release [[alpha-particle|alpha]] particles, [[beta-particle|beta]] particles or [[gamma-ray|gamma]] rays. Watch the names: they are three different things, not three sizes of one thing. Alpha and beta are particles, and gamma is not.

data.title: Alpha: a chunk
data.body: An alpha particle is a chunk: 2 protons and 2 neutrons stuck together. That is exactly the nucleus of a helium atom, with no electrons. It is a big, heavy particle.

data.title: Beta: a fast electron
data.body: A beta particle is a fast-moving particle. In the basic picture it is a fast electron. It is far lighter than an alpha particle, which is a whole chunk of the nucleus.

data.title: Gamma: not a particle
data.body: Gamma is not a particle at all. It is [[electromagnetic-radiation|electromagnetic radiation]], like light but far more energetic. Light is electromagnetic radiation too, so light and gamma belong to the same family.

data.task: Read each clue and pick the kind of radiation. Then watch it leave.

cases.clue: A chunk of 2 protons and 2 neutrons leaves the nucleus.
A fast electron leaves the nucleus.
High-energy electromagnetic radiation leaves the nucleus.

data.hint: Think about what each kind is made of.

data.title: Go deeper: what changes
data.body: Alpha and beta change the make-up of the nucleus, so a different nucleus is left. In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron is emitted, along with a tiny particle left out here. Gamma releases extra energy and changes neither the protons nor the neutrons.

data.title: Look around you
data.body: Look at anything near you, like a cup, a phone or your own hand. All of it is [[matter|matter]], and all matter is built from tiny pieces called [[atom|atoms]]. Light and heat are different: they are energy, and energy is not made of atoms. So for anything you meet, ask one question: is it matter, or is it energy?

data.title: Air is matter too
data.body: Air feels like nothing because you cannot see it, but it is matter too. You can show it: a pumped-up ball weighs more than a flat one. The only thing that changed is the air inside, so air must be made of atoms that have weight.

data.title: Far too small to see
data.body: So if everything is made of atoms, why can't we see them? Because they are extremely small. Zoom in on a skin cell and you are still far from an atom. An ordinary microscope uses light, and light is too coarse to show something that small.

data.task: Zoom in from your hand down to a single atom. Tap each stop.

stops.label: A hand
stops.note: You can see and hold this.

stops.label: A skin cell
stops.note: Too small to see without a microscope.

stops.label: A virus
stops.note: About 300 times smaller than the cell. It takes a strong microscope to see one.

stops.label: An atom
stops.sizeLabel: a few tenths of a nm
stops.note: About 300 times smaller again than a virus.

data.speaker: npc-hal
data.title: An idea before the proof
data.body: About 2,400 years ago the Greek thinker Democritus asked what would happen if you kept cutting something in half. He imagined a smallest piece that could not be cut, and called it atomos. Seeing atoms took far longer.

data.title: Three questions, three units
data.body: Picture a cloud, a bucket and a garden. The cloud drops rain. The bucket catches some. The garden may or may not be harmed by it. Radiation has three questions like that, and each one has its own unit.

data.title: Becquerel: how active the source is
data.body: The [[becquerel|becquerel]] tells you how active a source is. One becquerel is one decay per second. So a source of 20 becquerels has 20 nuclei decaying every second.

data.title: A big number is about the source
data.body: A becquerel counts what the source is doing, like the cloud counting its drops. It does not say how much radiation reached you, or what it did. Those have their own units.

data.title: Gray: energy absorbed
data.body: The [[gray|gray]] measures energy absorbed, like the water in the bucket. One gray is one joule of energy absorbed by each kilogram. It does not say what kind of radiation the energy came from.

data.title: Sievert: potential for harm
data.body: The [[sievert|sievert]] measures the potential for harm, like what the rain does to the garden. It counts the energy absorbed, and also the type of radiation and how sensitive the tissue is.

data.title: Go deeper: older units
data.body: Older names are still used. The curie measures activity like the becquerel, the rad measures absorbed dose like the gray, and the rem measures biological effect like the sievert. 100 rem is one sievert.

data.title: Not always finished
data.body: A nucleus decays into a daughter. But the daughter does not have to be stable. If it is unstable too, it decays again, and then again. So one decay is not always the end.

data.task: Tap the unstable nucleus to make it change. Keep going until it is stable.
data.hint: If the app says it isn't finished yet, tap again.

data.title: A decay chain
data.body: A [[decay-chain|decay chain]] is a sequence of radioactive decays: one nucleus changes into another, which may decay again. It ends only when a stable nucleus is reached, because a stable nucleus has nothing left to change into.

data.title: Nothing vanishes
data.body: Look at what each step does. A decay does not make an atom disappear. It changes the nucleus into a different nucleus, and that different nucleus is what is left behind. One unstable nucleus can start a whole chain of these changes.

data.title: Go deeper: real chains
data.body: Real decay chains exist in nature. The uranium-238 chain ends in stable lead-206. The thorium-232 chain ends in stable lead-208. Some steps can branch in more than one way. There is nothing to memorise.

data.title: A puzzle in an empty field
data.body: Here is a puzzle. You switch on a radiation detector in an empty field. Nothing radioactive is anywhere near. The detector still shows a small reading. Is it broken?

data.title: Background radiation
data.body: [[background-radiation|Background radiation]] is present on Earth at all times. It comes mostly from natural minerals in the ground, soil and water, and from cosmic radiation. So a working detector picks up a little almost anywhere.

data.title: Inside a Geiger counter
data.body: A [[geiger-counter|Geiger counter]] has a tube of gas. When radiation passes through, it ionizes the gas. The counter detects that ionization.

data.title: More radiation, more counts
data.body: The rate of ionization goes with the amount of radiation. A little radiation gives a few counts, and more radiation gives many more. Background radiation varies from place to place, so the reading does too.

data.title: Three instruments
data.body: A Geiger counter detects ionization in a gas. A scintillation counter turns flashes of light into a signal. A dosimeter is worn by a person to measure how much radiation they are exposed to.

data.title: Fast or slow
data.body: How fast a dose arrives is called the [[dose-rate|dose rate]]. It is given in units such as microsieverts per hour or millisieverts per year. The same amount can arrive in minutes or over many years.

data.title: Your guess, answered
data.body: A very high dose in a short time is the dangerous case. The same total spread over a long time is much less risky, because the cells have time to repair damage in between. Effects are more severe at higher doses and higher dose rates.

data.title: A big dose, quickly
data.body: About 1 sievert, or 1000 millisieverts, in a short time is the threshold for [[acute-radiation-syndrome|acute radiation syndrome]]. Within hours it can cause symptoms such as nausea and vomiting. High doses can also cause skin redness, hair loss and burns.

data.title: Small doses, spread out
data.body: Low levels of radiation do not cause immediate health effects. They can add a small increase in the risk of cancer over a lifetime. If a dose is low or spread over a long time, the risk is lower, because repair is more likely.

data.title: Go deeper: a one-time 100
data.body: About 99 in 100 people given a one-time dose of 100 millisieverts would not get cancer as a result. At that dose, extra cancers caused by radiation would be extremely difficult to identify.

data.title: What makes gold gold?
data.body: Gold, oxygen and carbon are very different, yet their atoms are built from the same three particles. What differs is the number of [[proton|protons]], and that tells you which [[element|element]] it is. 6 protons is always carbon, 7 is always nitrogen and 8 is always oxygen. Like a name tag, the protons say which element it is.

data.task: This atom has 6 protons, so it is carbon. Add one proton and watch the element.

data.title: Change the protons, change the element
data.body: So what happens if the number changes? Add a proton to carbon and you get nitrogen, which is a different element. The neutrons and electrons do not decide the element. Only the protons do.

data.task: Now this atom has 7 protons: nitrogen. Add one more to turn it into oxygen.

data.title: Go deeper: the periodic table
data.body: The [[periodic-table|periodic table]] lists every element in order of its number of protons. Each box shows that number, a short symbol and the name. You do not need to memorise it.

data.title: About half have changed
data.body: Picture 100 radioactive nuclei in a box. Wait a while, and about half of them will have changed. The time that takes is called the [[half-life|half-life]]. Nothing was cut in half: about 50 nuclei changed, and about 50 did not.

data.title: The numbers are a pattern
data.body: Keep waiting and the pattern repeats. Start with 100. After one half-life about 50 are left, after two about 25, then about 12, then about 6. Each time, half of what is left changes. It says about because each count is a pattern and not an exact number.

data.title: A group, not a timer
data.body: Remember: you cannot say when one nucleus will change. A big group is different, because it follows a pattern. Half-life describes the whole group. It is not a timer inside each atom, so one nucleus might change in a moment or much later.

data.title: Some fade fast, some very slowly
data.body: Half-lives are very different. Some are a fraction of a second. Others are billions of years. So some radioactive materials fade quickly and others take a very long time. You do not need to memorise these.

figure.caption: The bars are not to scale: each step is far bigger than it looks.

data.title: Go deeper: the decay curve
data.body: Plot the nuclei left against time and you get a curve that halves every half-life. It gets close to zero without a sharp end. This is called exponential decay. Each material has its own decay constant, a number for how fast it decays.

data.title: Radiation is energy on the move
data.body: Radiation is energy that travels. It can travel as waves, or as tiny particles. Sunlight is radiation, and so are radio waves and gamma rays.

data.title: Energy can hit an atom
data.body: Think of a ball rolling into a marble. A fast ball can knock the marble away. Some radiation hits an atom a bit like that, and knocks an electron right out of it.

data.title: That is ionization
data.body: Knocking an electron out of an atom is called ionization. Radiation with enough energy to do it is called [[ionizing-radiation|ionizing radiation]]. Weaker radiation can make atoms move or vibrate, but it cannot take an electron away.

data.title: Four ionizing kinds
data.body: Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and [[x-ray|X-rays]] are all ionizing. Alpha and beta are particles. Gamma rays and X-rays are waves of energy.

data.title: Three that are not
data.body: Visible light, microwaves and radio waves are not ionizing. They do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms. They are still radiation, so the word radiation alone does not tell you which kind you have.

data.title: Go deeper: the line is not sharp
data.body: Ultraviolet light sits close to the line between the two groups. High-energy ultraviolet is ionizing, and lower-energy ultraviolet is not. Visible light is on the safe side of it.

data.title: A torch and a pot of glitter
data.body: Shine a torch at someone and the light reaches them. Switch it off, or step out of the beam, and it stops. Now tip a pot of glitter onto their sleeve. The glitter stays, even after they walk away. Radiation can act like the torch. Radioactive material can act like the glitter.

data.title: Exposed: in the path
data.body: You are exposed when you are in the path of radiation from a source. A medical X-ray is a source outside the body. When the radiation stops reaching you, the exposure is over.

data.title: Contaminated: material on or in
data.body: [[radioactive-contamination|Contamination]] is radioactive material on or in something, where it is not wanted. It can be on skin or clothes, breathed in or swallowed, or spread about a place.

data.title: The glitter is the problem
data.body: Radiation does not get on or in people. It is the material that spreads. That is how a person can be exposed to a source without being contaminated.

data.title: When does it end?
data.body: Near a source, the exposure ends when you move away or the source is shielded. If radioactive material is on you, you are exposed until it is removed, and material on skin or clothes can often be washed off. If it is inside you, you are exposed until it leaves the body.

data.title: Sealed or not
data.body: Radioactive material in a sealed source stays in its container. Material that is not sealed might be spread onto other objects.

data.title: Two carbons, two weights
data.body: Here is a puzzle. Two atoms are both carbon, but one is heavier. How? Carbon atoms always have 6 protons, but the number of neutrons can differ: carbon-12 has 6 and carbon-14 has 8. The protons decide the element, so both are carbon. These versions of one element are called [[isotope|isotopes]].

data.task: Make carbon-14 from carbon-12 by adding 2 neutrons.
data.hint: Carbon-12 has 6 neutrons. Tap + two times. The protons did not change, so it is still carbon.

data.title: Isotope does not mean radioactive
data.body: Many people hear 'isotope' and think 'radioactive', but isotope only means a version of an element. Carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, and most of the atoms around you are stable isotopes. Carbon-14 is one of the few that is not.

data.title: Go deeper: reading the name
data.body: The number after the name is the [[mass-number|mass number]]: protons plus neutrons. Carbon has 6 protons, so carbon-14 has 14 - 6 = 8 neutrons.

data.title: Three particles
data.body: Every atom is built from just three kinds of particle. [[proton|Protons]] are positive, [[electron|electrons]] are negative, and [[neutron|neutrons]] have no charge, which is how they got their name. Different elements are made from the same three particles, only in different numbers.

data.task: Build a helium atom: 2 protons, 2 neutrons and 2 electrons.
data.hint: Add particles with the plus buttons. Helium has two of each.

data.title: A tiny centre
data.body: The protons and neutrons are packed together in a tiny centre called the [[nucleus|nucleus]]. The electrons are outside it, and that leaves a lot of room between them. So the nucleus is only a speck, and the atom is mostly empty space.

data.title: The stadium, answered
data.body: If an atom were a football stadium, its nucleus would be a marble in the middle. The electrons would be far out, and the rest is mostly empty space. The marble is tiny, but it holds the protons and neutrons, so almost all of the atom's mass is packed into it.

data.speaker: npc-hal
data.title: How do we know?
data.body: [[ernest-rutherford|Ernest Rutherford]]'s team fired tiny particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, so atoms must be mostly empty. A few bounced straight back, so each atom must have a tiny, heavy centre.

data.title: Not tiny planets
data.body: Pictures often show electrons on neat rings, like planets. A better picture is an [[electron-cloud|electron cloud]]: the electrons are somewhere in a fuzzy region around the nucleus.

data.title: A puzzle
data.body: Ionizing radiation carries enough energy to affect the atoms in living cells. That means it can damage a cell's [[dna|DNA]], its genetic material. Yet you get a small dose every day and you are not ill. Why not?

data.title: What radiation can do to a cell
data.body: When ionizing radiation passes through a cell, it can hit the atoms inside it. If it hits the DNA, the DNA is damaged. The cell has to deal with that damage.

data.title: Cells repair themselves
data.body: The answer to the puzzle is repair. Cells are extremely efficient at repairing this kind of damage, and they do it all the time. A small amount of damage is usually put right.

data.title: Exposed is not radioactive
data.body: Being exposed to radiation is not the same as carrying a radioactive source. A person who was exposed is not radioactive. Radiation does not get on or in people.

data.speaker: npc-ada
data.title: A discovery that wasn't supposed to happen
data.body: [[henri-becquerel|Henri Becquerel]] left a uranium mineral on a wrapped photographic plate and found it fogged, even with no sunlight. Radioactivity was found in a natural mineral, long before people made any nuclear technology.

data.title: Rocks and soil
data.body: Rocks and soil contain some natural radioactive materials, such as uranium and thorium. This is why the ground gives off a little radiation. It has been this way since long before people.

data.title: In the air
data.body: Radioactive materials in the ground can produce [[radon|radon]], a radioactive gas. Radon is in the air outside, and it can get into buildings.

data.title: Food and your body
data.body: Your body contains a little natural radioactive potassium, called [[potassium-40|potassium-40]]. So do many foods, such as bananas. It is a tiny share of all your potassium.

data.title: From space
data.body: Earth is hit by [[cosmic-radiation|cosmic radiation]] from space all the time. It is one more part of the [[background-radiation|radiation around us]].

data.title: It depends
data.body: Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous. What matters is the type of radiation, how much there is, and how it reaches the body. A banana and your own body are radioactive, and that is normal. Later you will see why being exposed to radiation is not the same as becoming radioactive.

data.title: Go deeper: radon and chains
data.body: Radon is one link in a natural decay chain that starts with uranium in rock. Potassium-40 is another natural radionuclide, found in food and the body. Natural chains like these were running long before people existed.

data.title: Three questions
data.body: A headline about radiation is only useful with three questions. How big is the dose, in millisieverts? How fast did it arrive? And how does it compare with doses you already know?

data.title: Put it on the scale
data.body: Compare a number with the doses you know. An average year is about 6 millisieverts. A whole body CT is about 10. Acute illness starts at about 1000, in a short time.

data.title: Two wrong answers
data.body: One wrong answer says any dose is deadly. The other says radiation is harmless. Both are wrong. A very large dose in a short time makes people ill, and low doses add a small chance of cancer over a lifetime. Size and speed decide.

data.title: Go deeper: a number to remember
data.body: About 1000 millisieverts in a short time is where illness starts. An average year is about 6. That is a gap of well over a hundred times.

data.title: Stable and unstable
data.body: Does an atom stay the same for ever? Most do. Some combinations of protons and neutrons make a stable nucleus, which stays as it is. Other combinations make an unstable nucleus, which can change. Most of the atoms around you, and in you, are stable.

data.task: Carbon-14 is unstable. Change the neutrons until the carbon atom is stable.
data.hint: Stable carbon has 6 or 7 neutrons. Tap - until the badge says Stable.

data.title: Unstable nuclei can change
data.body: An unstable nucleus can change into a different nucleus. When it does, it gives off [[radiation|radiation]]. This is called [[radioactivity|radioactivity]], and an atom that does it is radioactive. It happens because the nucleus is unstable, not because anyone makes it happen.

data.title: Radioactivity is natural
data.body: Nobody had to invent radioactivity. Unstable atoms are in rocks, in the air and in food. A banana and your own body hold a little natural potassium-40. People can make radioactive atoms too, but most of the radioactivity around us is natural.

data.title: What comes next
data.body: So now you know that some nuclei can change all by themselves. In the next unit you will find out what comes out when one does, and how fast it happens.

data.title: Go deeper: what holds a nucleus together
data.body: Protons are all positive, so they push each other apart. A very strong force inside the nucleus, the [[strong-force|strong force]], helps hold it together. Some nuclei hold together well. Others do not.

data.title: How a dose is counted
data.body: Radiation is all around us, so the question is always how much. A dose measures how much radiation a body has taken in, and it is counted in [[sievert|sieverts]]. Everyday doses are tiny, so they are given in millisieverts: 1 sievert is 1000 [[millisievert|millisieverts]].

data.title: A little, every day
data.body: Everyone gets a small dose all the time. In the United States the average is about 6.2 millisieverts a year, and most of it is natural [[background-radiation|background radiation]]. Rocks, soil, space and [[radon|radon]] in the air all add to it.

data.title: From tiny to huge
data.body: Put some doses in a line. Living beside a nuclear power station for a year adds under 0.01 millisieverts. A year of cosmic rays at sea level is about 0.3, and radon in an average home about 2.3. One whole body CT is about 10. About 1000 in a short time is where people start to become ill.

data.title: Go deeper: where you live
data.body: Altitude changes the dose. Living in Denver, about 5,280 feet up, adds about 0.8 millisieverts a year from cosmic radiation, compared with about 0.3 at sea level. Where you live changes your yearly dose a little.

data.title: You can lower a dose
data.body: A dose is not fixed. There are three ways to lower it: spend less time near the source, stay farther from it, or put a shield between you and it. Time, distance and shielding.

data.title: Less time
data.body: Limiting the time you are exposed reduces the dose from the source. A shorter visit near a source means a smaller dose.

data.title: More distance
data.body: The dose decreases dramatically as you increase your distance from the source. Stepping farther away lowers it a lot.

data.title: Something in between
data.body: Shielding means putting material between you and the source. Barriers of lead, concrete or water protect from penetrating gamma rays, and a good shield can greatly reduce or remove the dose.

data.title: Where you see them
data.body: Dentists place a lead apron on patients having X-rays of their teeth. Radioactive materials are stored under water, in concrete, or in lead-lined rooms. In a shelter, more walls give more protection.

data.title: Alpha: heavy, so it stops fast
data.body: An alpha particle is heavy. A heavy particle uses up its energy over a very short distance. So a sheet or two of paper, or the top layer of your skin, usually stops it.

data.title: Beta: small and fast
data.body: A beta particle is small and fast. It goes farther through air than an alpha particle, and it passes through paper. A thin layer of metal, such as aluminum, stops it.

data.title: Gamma: very penetrating
data.body: Gamma rays are pure energy, and they are very penetrating. They pass through skin and clothing. Paper and a thin layer of metal will not stop them.

data.title: What it takes to stop gamma
data.body: It takes several inches of a dense material like lead, or a few feet of concrete, to stop gamma rays. Thick and dense: that is what makes a good shield against them.

data.title: Go deeper: shields at work
data.body: Barriers of lead, concrete or water protect against gamma rays and X-rays. That is why some radioactive materials are stored under water, or in concrete or lead-lined rooms, and why a dentist puts a lead apron on you.

data.title: Left alone, it still changes
data.body: An unstable nucleus can change all by itself, even when nobody does anything to it, because the instability is already inside it. It does not vanish. It turns into a different nucleus and gives off [[radiation|radiation]].

data.title: Parent and daughter
data.body: Scientists give the two nuclei names. The nucleus that changes is the [[parent-nuclide|parent]]. The nucleus it becomes is the [[daughter-nuclide|daughter]]. The change gives off radiation, and that radiation is what comes out.

data.title: Random for one, regular for many
data.body: You can say that a nucleus has a chance of changing. You cannot say when. Watch one nucleus and its moment is a surprise, and no nucleus ever gets 'due'. A whole group is different, and the next lessons show how.

data.title: Go deeper: what can change it?
data.body: An unstable nucleus is called a [[radionuclide|radionuclide]]. When it changes, a different nuclide can result, and energy leaves as particles or electromagnetic radiation. Heating, cooling and chemistry hardly change how fast this happens. In a flame or in ice, it is still unstable.
